It's an easy conclusion to reach. You read an input exactly like a

the same way. Decorator inputs built the habit: an

compiled and the number on screen changed. But that write never reached the parent, and the next time the parent's bound value changed, Angular overwrote it without a word. Decorator inputs always followed the same rule as signal inputs. Signal inputs just put it in the type.
An input is the parent's value, delivered
, Angular evaluates the binding, writes the result into the child's input, and does it again each time the bound value changes. The
the child receives is a read-only window on that delivery: it always holds the latest value the parent bound, and it has no

. If the child could write it, the value would have two writers and no rule for who wins. The parent would keep showing its own number, and its next update would silently erase the child's. One value with one owner is the
rule, and the type enforces it.
So "how do I set my input?" is the wrong question. The useful one is: who owns the edit?
